To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) agents trained to access and execute instructions are able to generalize their behavior to instructions that are not experienced during training; (ii) agents trained to ignore objects develop a different semantic space than agents trained to access objects; (iii) the composition of the agents’ behavioral set influences the development of their semantic structure.

the development of a systematized semantic space, grounded on the agents sensory motor capabilities, and the capability to temporally decompose linguistic instructions, are the key factors underlying the ability to generalize behavior in evolving robots.

the emergence of linguistic compositionality in a population of agents controlled by dynamically coupled recurrent neural networks is possible, that this emergence depends on the behavioral repertoire of the agent, and that it is grounded on a systematized semantic space.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a system of semantic representation that is grounded in the sensory-motor capabilities of the agents and that is organized to facilitate the emergence of linguistic compositionality.
the emergence of compositional semantics and behavioral generalization in populations of evolving autonomous agents.
the development of a model of the emergence of linguistic compositionality and of behavioral generalization in evolving robots.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the development of semantic spaces in neural networks is not a simple consequence of their sensory motor capabilities but it is rather a complex phenomenon that is influenced by several factors, such as the behavioral set and the compositionality of the instructions.

the development of semantic structures is a consequence of the development of the agent's behavioral capabilities and that the development of the behavioral capabilities is in turn influenced by the composition of the agent's set of behavioral skills.

the emergence of linguistic compositionality is not a simple byproduct of the evolution of linguistic capabilities, but it is the result of a complex interplay between the agent's sensory motor capabilities, the structure of the environment, and the behavioral requirements of the task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the emergence of compositionality and generalization are not only possible in a population of agents but they are also strongly dependent on the agents’ behavior.

we have shown that the evolution of linguistic compositionality and the emergence of semantic structures can be observed in a population of agents controlled by dynamcial neural networks, provided they have a sufficiently rich behavioral repertoire and a sensory motor system capable of representing the world and of grounding the linguistic input.

we have shown that the development of linguistic compositionality and of behavioral generalization in a population of evolving robots can be explained by the emergence of a semantic space that is grounded in the sensory-motor capability of the agents and that is organized in a systemized way to allow for efficient access and execution of linguistic instructions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the emergence of compositionality in a system is not a trivial consequence of the mere existence of a symbolic representation.
the emergence of linguistic compositional semantics is not only possible, but can be observed in the behavior of agents with a limited sensory motor repertoire.
the development of compositality and generalization can be achieved by means of artificial evolution, without requiring a priori assumptions about the structure of the semantic spaces.
